title: The lamp of the eye (Luke 11:14–36)
hook: take heed that the light in you is not darkness

segments.voice: Yesterday, a friend at midnight kept knocking on a barred door for three loaves. Your line was shamelessly ask. Did you ask for the help you needed? Day five hundred forty-five.

This part of Luke is noisy. Jesus heals a man who couldn't speak, and some in the crowd say he does it by the power of the prince of demons. He answers that a house divided against itself falls. A woman shouts a blessing on his mother. Others demand a sign from heaven before they'll believe anything. Accusations, arguments, people shouting from the back. And in the middle of all that heat, he stops and talks about something quiet: a lamp in a room, and the light that comes in through your eyes.

First, the lamp. Nobody lights one and hides it under a bushel; you set it on a stand so whoever walks in can see. Then, in the King James Bible: "The light of the body is the eye: therefore when thine eye is single, thy whole body also is full of light; but when thine eye is evil, thy body also is full of darkness." Single sounds odd to us. The Greek word, haplous, means simple, whole, undivided: an eye that sees clearly because it isn't split between ten things. And here's a detail that changes how it sounds. In Jesus' world, a good eye and an evil eye were also ways of talking about money and people. A generous person had a good eye; a stingy, envious one had an evil eye. Proverbs says it this way: "He that hath a bountiful eye shall be blessed; for he giveth of his bread to the poor." Paul later uses a word from the same family as haplous for generosity. So the saying is about more than eyesight. How you look at people fills you up. Look at the world with envy or suspicion, and the darkness gets inside. Look with a clear, generous eye, and you fill with light. Then the warning, short and sharp: "Take heed therefore that the light which is in thee be not darkness." It's possible to think you're seeing clearly and be wrong. In a chapter full of people who looked straight at a healing and saw the devil, that line lands hard. The crowd wanted a sign from the sky. He points them back to their own eyes.
screen: `A GOOD EYE IS A GENEROUS EYE.`
then, large: `THE LIGHT OF THE BODY IS THE EYE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at something beautiful. Find one thing in front of you, or out of a window: a tree, a face in a photo, the light on a wall, a cup. Let your eyes rest on it, and only on it. When your attention splits, bring it back. Look at it generously, the way you'd look at something you love, without judging it or wanting anything from it. Notice what happens inside you as you look. If you pray, you can give thanks for what you see. The bell holds the time.
Haplous, Greek for single, simple, whole: Jesus says the eye is the body's light, and a clear, generous eye like that fills you with light, while an envious one lets the darkness in.
Your line: keep the light in. Today, when you catch yourself looking at someone with envy or suspicion, look again, on purpose, with a generous eye. Day five hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Some Christians practice a slow, attentive looking as prayer, with icons in Orthodox churches, with art and nature in many retreat traditions, and with the Ignatian habit of noticing where God was present in the day.

fork.setup: a crowd has just watched a man healed. some say it's the devil's work; others demand a sign from heaven. what does Jesus point them to?
options: their own eyes, and the light already in them.
fork.reveal: he talks about a lamp and says the light of the body is the eye: "take heed therefore that the light which is in thee be not darkness."

original.note: Greek: single, simple, whole. the King James Bible says single; a related word means generosity.

trapdoor: what you thought: a saying about having good eyesight.
what it means: how you look at the world and at people fills you with light or with darkness.
what a scholar hears: a good eye and an evil eye were idioms for generosity and stinginess, and haplous belongs to a word family that also means generosity.
